newsitem.title: USA: COMEX copper ends lower, but volumes light.
newsitem.headline: COMEX copper ends lower, but volumes light.

text.p: COMEX copper futures ended lower Thursday after a further rise in LME and COMEX warehouse stocks, but volume was light with copper market activity dampened by the May Day holiday in Europe, traders said.

"The recent backwardations in both COMEX and LME have been attracting supplies, but in the longer term U.S. economic growth and good Chinese economic growth is likely to continue to underpin prices," said Malcolm Freeman a senior trader with GNI Ltd in New York.
LME copper stocks rose a further 2,000 tonnes Thursday to 145,750 tonnes, while COMEX stocks slipped fell another 1,365 short tons Wednesday to 49,520 short tons.
COMEX July copper ended down 1.50 cents at 109.85 cents a lb after trading from 111.75 to 109.25 cents.
Estimated final volume for COMEX copper was 7,000 lots.
Daily momentum oscillators in COMEX July copper suggested the late April rally had begun to wane, analysts said, after nearby COMEX copper saw an eight month high around 119.60 cents in late March.
"But with volatility remaining high and a supply surplus looking unlikely this year, funds remain long, though they may have to wait a few months for a big move," Freeman said.
Annualized 20-day historical volatility was around 22 percent Thursday, while 14-day average true range for the July contract edged up to 2.01 cents a day.

The May/July spread ended little changed around 1.00 cent a pound, while the LME cash-to-three month spread was around $80.00 a tonne, after both spreads eased sharply in the past week as prompt market tightness dissipated.
But the COMEX July/September spread remained firmly backwardated around 3.10 cents.
Potential supply disruptions were still being watched also, traders said, after a second strike by workers at Chilean copper mines Wednesday .
Workers at Quebrada Blanca, which produces 75,000 tonnes of cathode a year, went on strike Wednesday after negotiations failed, local union president Nelson Fuentes said.
A small group of workers at the huge Escondida mine, also in Chile, have been on strike for over a week and a half.

On the demand side, the chairman of ASARCO, the world's fourth largest non-state-owned copper company, said Wednesday that the copper market would end 1997 and 1998 with supply/demand deficits of 53,000 short tons and 149,000 short tons respectively.
